paper_title: Energy-Tweedie: Score meets Score, Energy meets Energy

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Denoising and score estimation are classically linked through Tweedie's formula, which relates the posterior mean under Gaussian noise to the Stein score of the noisy marginal. In this work, we extend this perspective beyond Gaussian noise to a broad class of Gibbs (energy-based) noise distributions, with the generalized Gaussian family as an example. We derive the Energy-Tweedie identity: when the denoising posterior is viewed through the lens of scoring rules, the path derivative of a kernel scoring rule defined by the noise potential recovers the Stein score of the noisy marginal. Thus, the familiar correspondence between Gaussian noise, posterior means, squared loss, and Tweedie's formula is lifted to a distributional correspondence between Gibbs noise distributions, full posterior laws, kernel scoring rules, and the Energy-Tweedie identity, which gives a Tweedie-style relation for each noise potential. Among its consequences, this identity gives a posterior-samples-to-score route to score estimation, yields a principled criterion for estimating unknown noise parameters, and enables diffusion-style sampling along user-chosen paths through the noise-parameter space, supplying the score-based perspective on recent generative methods trained with scoring rules.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Denoising, empirical Bayes, and score-based generative modeling are classically tied together by Tweedies formula. Under additive Gaussian noise = + ϵ, the posterior mean E[X = y] is the MSE-optimal denoiser and its residual determines the Stein score sm(y) = log m(y) of the noisy marginal. This correspondence is one reason Gaussian denoising occupies such central position in score-based diffusion. Once the noise is non-Gaussian, however, the posterior mean is typically no longer the natural object exposed by the score. Our main result, the Energy-Tweedie identity, connects the score of the noisy marginal to the path derivative of scoring rule determined by the noise potential (such as the energy score), and evaluated at the denoising posterior.2 The familiar correspondence between Gaussian noise, posterior means, squared loss, and Tweedies formula is thus lifted to correspondence between Gibbs noise, full posterior laws, kernel scoring rules, and the Energy-Tweedie identity, as established in Theorem 4.1. Cor. 4.3 provides summary of the correspondence using the contrast between the Gaussian and generalized Gaussian cases. The main contributions of this work are thus: general identity. The Energy-Tweedie identity provides the noisy-marginal score for any normalizable Gibbs noise distribution (Thm. 4.1), establishing connection between the former and scoring rules. 1 Code repository: https://github.com/andleb/et. previously-unrelated homonyms: both energy and score have double meanings. 2 Somewhat coincidentally, we thus connect two pairs of 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). posterior-samples-to-score route. Any sufficiently accurate sampler of the denoising posterior becomes score estimator. Noise-parameter estimation. We propose an M-estimation method recovering all the unknown noise parameters of any Gibbs noise distribution from noisy data, with theoretical guarantees for the generalized Gaussian case. Diffusion along noise-parameter paths. We show how posterior models can be used inside traditional score-based samplers beyond Gaussian noising, with the path through the noise parameters design variable chosen freely at sampling time.

Despite this, matching the energy score to the noise-parameter path at training might prove useful: for example, when β 1, the energy score will encourage robustness to extreme values, which are likely to come up at that step due to the noising distribution. Subsequent to the preprint versions of this work, Martorella et al. [22] modify the energy-score parameters of scoring-rule diffusion model along the diffusion schedule while keeping isotropic Gaussian noise, and report improved few-step generation at ImageNet scale, in particular when only βt varies. Plugging the Energy-Tweedie score into an annealed Langevin sampler thus yields diffusion-style procedure over noise-parameter path. In the isotropic Gaussian case, this can be viewed through the usual reverse-SDE interpretation from ordinary diffusion [39] as the Energy-Tweedie identity (Eq. 21) simplifies to the Tweedie identity; in the general case, it should be viewed as score-based MCMC over sequence of intermediate targets as was the original perspective in NCSN/SMLD [37]. The use of scoring rules for diffusion-like generative modeling has been explored in Reverse Markov Learning [36] and Distributional Diffusion Models with Scoring Rules [8]. In contrast to the procedure above, neither runs score-based generation procedure; RML uses ancestral sampling and is thus roughly analogous to DDPM, while De Bortoli et al. [8] employ an approach analogous to DDIM using the learned full posterior p(x0 xt). Our proposed approach thus provides the missing score-based perspective analogous to NCSN/SMLD. We reuse the Eight-Gaussians posterior model of Sec. 5.1 and train corresponding one on MNIST [20], both conditioned on η = (β, λ, σ, u, v). Through Eq. 32, each model supplies the EnergyTweedie score anywhere in the noise-parameter space, and hence along an arbitrary noise-parameter path (cid:55) (βt, λt, Σt) instead of single scalar noise schedule. Figure 1 displays the learned score field for the Eight-Gaussians data as each parameter is varied in turn; in particular, the mean-seeking Gaussian field (β = 2) concentrates mass toward the ring, while for β < 2 the field tends toward the geometric-median regime and targets the mixture centers directly, as discussed in Sec. 3.1. The displayed base parameter combination is (β, λ, ρ, u, v) = (1.4, 1.8, 0.57, 0, 0.6) (ρ is the reference RMS of Eq. 42). For generation, we run annealed Langevin over four reverse paths through the Figure 1: Energy-Tweedie score fields from the five-parameter Eight-Gaussians posterior model as each noise parameter is varied. The colorbar represents the score magnitude (log scale). noise-parameter space, matched in noise RMS: an isotropic fixed-tail reference, fixed non-diagonal covariance, covariance completing full rotation, and joint path along which all five parameters vary simultaneously. The path definitions, setup and more results are given in App. A.6.1. The same construction carries over to MNIST. We examine five paths with common noise magnitude: four fixed combinations of Gaussian or generalized radial law with isotropic or non-diagonal covariance, together with jointly varying path that transforms Gaussian diffusion continuously into heavy-tailed anisotropic one (definitions in App. A.6.2). Figure 2 shows unselected samples from all five paths, each producing recognizable, class-diverse digits. On quantitative metrics (Table 13 in App. A.6.2), the generalized/non-diagonal path attains the best point estimates on all metrics. As the model, noise magnitude schedule and sampling budget are shared, this comparison shows that the noise-parameter path, enabled by the Energy-Tweedie identity, is consequential modeling choice. Additional results are presented in App. A.6. sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Classical work on Tweedie-type identities and empirical Bayes goes back to Robbins [29] and refinements such as Efron [10]. Score matching [15; 38] provides way to estimate score fields and forms the basis of modern score-based generative modeling [39]. Self-supervised denoising handles unknown noise mainly either through risk surrogates or through Tweedie-based score extraction. SURE-type methods estimate or optimize denoising risk under Gaussian noise, with UNSURE relaxing the need to know the noise level [40; 43]. Noise2Score and Noise-Distribution Adaptive Denoising instead estimate the noisy marginal score using denoising autoencoder machinery and plug it into classic Tweedie formulas [17; 18]. The use of denoising autoencoders provides contrast to recent work on energy-score-based autoencoders [34], for which non-asymptotic score alignment has been established [19], albeit in different setting. Estimation of unknown noise parameters has typically been indirect, relying on surrogates such as reconstructed-image regularity (cf. Sec. 5.2). In addition to the scoring-rule-based diffusion approaches discussed in Sec. 5.3, heavy-tailed diffusion methods replace Gaussian perturbations with richer noising processes: Yoon et al. [47] use isotropic α-stable Lévy processes and fractional denoising score matching, Shariatian et al. [33] give DDPMstyle construction with α-stable noise, and Pandey et al. [26] use Student-t perturbations to model heavy-tailed data. These works modify the forward noising process or reverse sampler, whereas our contribution is score identity. For Student-t noise in particular, Cor. 4.4 supplies the corresponding identity and matched kernel score. Concurrent work also links generative modeling to score-induced geometry: Energy Matching [1] uses an interaction term to ensure diversity (conceptually similar to the energy score), and an optimal-transport term to encourage direct paths to the data manifold, which we observe for β 1; dual score matching [14] learns normalized image energies whose spatial gradient is the score; and the InformationEstimation Metric [25] builds data-dependent distances by comparing denoising-error or score fields over Gaussian noise scales. In our case the metric is tied to the additive noise law, and the identity singles out mean β-energy (App. A.7.1).

sections.title: 7 Discussion
sections.content: This work generalizes the Gaussian Tweedie correspondence from posterior-mean identity to distributional identity that holds for any additive Gibbs noise. The main object is the denoising posterior viewed through kernel score induced by the noise potential. The resulting Energy-Tweedie identity then gives the score of the noisy marginal as the path-derivative of this matched scoring rule, with the noise potential alone determining propriety. The classical results are recovered in the Gaussian case. The identity gives posterior-sample route to score estimation, turns the estimation of unknown noise parameters (for any Gibbs noise) into an M-estimation problem that moves beyond estimating scalar noise level, and provides the missing score-based view of distributional diffusion approaches, where the process can be non-Gaussian, and the noise-parameter schedule becomes path chosen freely at sampling time. These consequences also suggest promising additional uses. In inverse problems [7], many approaches use the score of noisy distributions, which Energy-Tweedie provides without the Gaussian assumption. Similarly, in test-time denoising under noise distribution shift, the discrepancy in Eq. 27 could be used to estimate candidate parameters. While the identity is general, we have focused on the generalized Gaussian family for the examples. The theory for parameter estimation currently assumes that the posterior is correctly specified and that the auxiliary score estimator is sufficiently accurate; relaxing these could be future direction. On the diffusion side, scaling to competitive large-scale image-generation benchmarks remains open.

sections.content: 1) Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract and introduction state the papers main contributions: the Energy Tweedie identity, its relationship to the classical setting, and its consequences for score estimation, noise-parameter estimation, and diffusion-style sampling. 2) Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The Discussion lists the limitations: the identity holds for the (large) additive Gibbs noise model, the noise-parameter estimation theory assumes correctly specified posterior term and sufficiently accurate auxiliary score estimator, the experiments are specialized to the generalized Gaussian case on low-dimensional synthetic data and MNIST, and large-scale image-generation benchmarks are out of scope. 3) Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The theoretical results state their assumptions in the main text or immediately adjacent discussion, and the formal proofs are provided in the appendix. 4) Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The experiments use well-known synthetic datasets and MNIST, and all the settings and steps needed to reproduce them are included. 5) Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The data used in the experiments are synthetically generated or public (MNIST); the code, configurations, trained models, and instructions for reproducing the experimental results are released at https://github.com/andleb/et. 6) Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We specify the main details in the paper and the rest in the appendix and the public code repository. 7) Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Where applicable, the reported experimental results include error bars or equivalent uncertainty summaries for the experiments supporting the empirical claims. 57 8) Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The compute resources used are documented in the public code repository. 9) Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The work conforms to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. 10) Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The work is primarily theoretical and methodological: it derives fundamental identities and validates them in controlled synthetic experiments. Accordingly, we do not identify direct negative societal impact beyond the general possibility that improved score estimation or generative-modeling methodology could eventually be incorporated into downstream systems. 11) Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not release high-risk pretrained model, dataset, image generator, or other asset requiring controlled access safeguards. 12) Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The public code repository documents the licenses of the software dependencies and third-party assets used to run the experiments. 13) New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper releases new experimental code, synthetic-data generation scripts, and configuration files needed to reproduce the results. 14) Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing or research with human subjects. 15) Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects 58 Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve human subjects research. 16) Declaration of LLM usage Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. Answer: [N/A] Justification: LLMs are not an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this work. The use of LLMs was limited to ordinary writing, editing, formatting, and basic code-assistance purposes and thus did not affect the core methodology or scientific claims.
